subject: biology

moments.title: Oparin and Haldane — primordial soup
moments.who: Alexander Oparin (Moscow) and J. B. S. Haldane (Cambridge) — independently
moments.body:
Both propose that early Earth's atmosphere was reducing (rich in hydrogen, methane, ammonia, water vapour), and that simple organic molecules could form spontaneously from these gases under ultraviolet light and lightning.

The resulting 'primordial soup' would contain amino acids, sugars, nucleotides. Over time, self-replicating molecules would emerge — and life would begin.
moments.takeaway: Life can in principle emerge from non-life. The hypothesis is articulated; it needs testing.

moments.title: Miller-Urey experiment
moments.who: Stanley Miller and Harold Urey, University of Chicago
moments.body:
Stanley Miller, a 23-year-old graduate student, builds a closed-loop apparatus with water (representing oceans), methane, ammonia and hydrogen (representing the atmosphere), with electric sparks (representing lightning). He runs it for a week.

The water turns brown. Analysis: 11 amino acids form, including alanine and glycine — the building blocks of proteins. From simple gases, simple chemistry under realistic conditions makes biology's monomers.

quote.text: Just turn on the spark and wait.

moments.takeaway: Building blocks of life form spontaneously under plausible early-Earth conditions.

moments.title: RNA world
moments.who: Walter Gilbert (Harvard), and others; Cech and Altman discover ribozymes
moments.body:
Thomas Cech (Colorado) and Sidney Altman (Yale) independently discover ribozymes — RNA molecules with catalytic activity (1982-83, Nobel 1989). RNA can both carry information AND catalyse reactions.

Walter Gilbert coins 'RNA world' (1986) for an early life stage where RNA did both jobs — predating DNA (better at information storage) and protein (better at catalysis). Modern ribosomes are essentially huge ribozymes — a vestige.
moments.takeaway: RNA can be both gene and enzyme. The RNA world is a plausible precursor to current biology.

moments.title: Hydrothermal vents
moments.body:
Submarine expeditions discover hydrothermal vents in the deep ocean. Bacterial communities live without sunlight, oxidising hydrogen sulfide from the vents. They support tubeworms, mussels, crabs — a complete ecosystem powered by Earth's interior, not the sun.

Mike Russell and Bill Martin propose (1990s-2000s) that life began at alkaline hydrothermal vents, where natural pH gradients across rocky mineral walls could have powered the first metabolism — like primitive ATP synthase machines.
moments.takeaway: Life can exist without sunlight. The origin of life may have been at hydrothermal vents — and proton gradients may have been the first energy source.

moments.title: LUCA and the tree of life
moments.who: Carl Woese, Bill Martin, Madeline Weiss and others
moments.body:
Sequencing extensive sets of universal genes (those present in all known life) yields a picture of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA). LUCA was likely a thermophile, anaerobe, that lived around hydrothermal vents about 4 billion years ago, used H2 and CO2 for metabolism, and had ribosomes already.

Weiss et al. (2016) identified ~355 genes likely present in LUCA. Life's deepest features — DNA-based information, RNA translation, ATP-based energy currency, lipid membranes — were already in place.
moments.takeaway: LUCA had most of modern biochemistry. The first life that gave rise to all known life was already complex. The earlier history is hidden.

now.title: Origin of life today
now.body:
Origin of life research has many threads: prebiotic chemistry (forming nucleotides from simple precursors — Sutherland's 2009 cyclic phosphate route), protocell assembly (Szostak's lab), RNA evolution in test tubes, alkaline vent geochemistry, ribosome evolution.

The Mars perseverance rover collects samples that may bear evidence of past microbial life. Europa, Enceladus and Titan are candidate sites for present-day life elsewhere.
now.open_questions: How did the first self-replicator arise? RNA, peptide, or both? Where (vent, pond, surface)? Could life have originated more than once on Earth (we'd never know — it would have been outcompeted)? Are we alone in the universe? What's the prebiotic plausibility of the genetic code's particular structure?

reflection: Origin of life is the most fundamental and least tractable question in biology. The relevant events happened 4 billion years ago, the relevant chemistry is buried under 4 billion years of subsequent change. How do we judge progress on a problem where we may never directly witness the answer, only constrain it from multiple angles?
